summary: Investigates security threats and risks for Open Pluggable Edge Services and how those threats affect the underlying architecture. It is for discovering and analyzing threats and does not specify or recommend solutions.

plainLanguage.summary: Before building a conveyor belt with helpers, you ask what mischief the helpers could do. This document lists the worries without fixing them.

questions: risks of open pluggable edge services
what are the security threats of opes
why does opes break end to end encryption
subtitle: A catalogue of what can go wrong when third-party services rewrite web traffic at the edge of the network.

tldr.problem: OPES lets processors and callout servers inspect and change application messages between a data provider and a data consumer, which creates new places for attackers and mistakes to do harm.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC walks through threats to the data flow (network level and application level) and to the out-of-band control data, describing each one from the point of view of the consumer and provider applications.
tldr.outcome: It is a threat analysis only. It does not specify or recommend any solutions, and can serve as input for similar thinking about web caches and CDNs.

today: RFC 3837 is an Informational RFC from August 2004 and has not been obsoleted or updated. It is a threat analysis that accompanies the OPES architecture in RFC 3835; it does not define a protocol.

sections.title: Introduction and Scope
sections.content:
The Open Pluggable Edge Services (OPES) architecture, defined in RFC 3835, lets OPES services work between a data provider, a data consumer and zero or more OPES processors. These services analyze and possibly transform application-level messages. A processor can hand work to one or more remote callout servers.

The RFC splits threats in two ways: by whom they hurt (consumer applications or provider applications) and by who causes them. Insiders are parties that are part of the OPES system; outsiders are not. Insiders can do harm through bad configuration, bad software or compromised networks.

The stated goal is threat discovery and analysis. The document does not specify or recommend solutions, and it only covers threats introduced by the OPES processor and callout servers, not those of content services that do not use OPES.
sections.plainLanguage: Some helpers will stand between you and your mail. This part says who might misbehave: people inside the system by accident or on purpose, and strangers outside it.

sections.title: Threats to the Data Flow
sections.content:
The architecture builds on widely adopted protocols and requires that an OPES processor SHALL NOT interfere with non-OPES aware clients and servers. That eases deployment, but most browsers cannot use safeguards added as protocol extensions, and a normal user cannot cheaply check where content really came from.

The RFC points out that an OPES processor combines a traffic interception point with high-performance code able to analyze and modify all passing data. That is exactly what a classic man-in-the-middle attack needs. A compromised processor or callout server can also ripple across every provider that uses the affected service.
sections.plainLanguage: Because the helper sits right in the middle of the belt and can see everything, a bad helper is very powerful. Most people would not even know it was there.

sections.title: Network-Level Threats
sections.content:
Processors and callout servers can be attacked from outside or from the networks of other OPES providers. Common application protocols give weak guarantees of privacy, authentication and integrity. The IAB considerations in RFC 3238 require that an OPES processor's IP address be reachable by data consumer applications, which limits putting it behind firewalls. Using TCP/IP exposes it to known attacks such as IP spoofing and session stealing.

Denial of service is a main concern: spurious requests from a malicious node can use up CPU, memory and network interfaces, and a distributed attack can do so from many nodes at once. An implementation that breaks end-to-end addressing or flow control could also endanger the wider network, for example by causing congestion.
sections.plainLanguage: If the helper has a front door anyone can knock on, people can knock so hard that nobody else gets served.

sections.title: Application-Level Threats
sections.content:
At the content level the RFC lists a series of risks. Insiders may act intentionally or by accident; outsiders are frequently intentional.

  • Unauthorized entities: authorization happens out of band, so finding an OPES entity and verifying it is hard.
  • Unauthorized actions: authorization covers transformation classes, not individual rules, so rules may do things they were not allowed to.
  • Unwanted transformations: for example ad flooding, or one party's filter changing the meaning of text.
  • Corrupted content: a compromised server may inject bogus content.
  • Message structure: adding or removing headers can break end-to-end integrity.
  • Complex data: inconsistent changes to related objects can break references.

Fine-grained permissions (for parts of a message) are hard to express and check, and the RFC says a fine-grained policy language should be devised, possibly enforced with digital signatures.
sections.plainLanguage: Helpers might open the wrong parcel, swap something inside, or make a mess of the labels. Even a well-meaning helper can break things.

sections.title: Encryption, Tracing and Authentication
sections.content:
OPES services generally cannot be applied to data protected with end-to-end encryption, because the decryption key cannot be shared with processors without compromising confidentiality. Services that modify data are also incompatible with end-to-end integrity protection. The RFC says extending the end-to-end model, or defining hop-by-hop integrity protection, is out of scope.

Tracing and notification facilities can be attacked, or may lack standards. Lack of strong authentication between processors and callout servers may open holes for DoS and other attacks.
sections.plainLanguage: A sealed envelope cannot be changed by a helper, so to let helpers work you must either leave it open or trust each helper in turn. Neither choice is perfect.

sections.title: Threats to Out-of-Band Data
sections.content:
OPES keeps the data flow separate from control information such as loading rulesets, trust establishment, tracing and policy propagation. Requirements exist for it but no mechanism is prescribed, which leaves implementers to make sure of data security, entity authentication and action authorization. The RFC lists these threats:

  • Weaknesses that open the door to the data flow attacks above.
  • Inaccurate accounting information, so consumers may be wrongly charged or providers unpaid.
  • Repudiation of service requests: a party makes an authorized request and later denies it.
  • Inconsistent privacy policy, including different jurisdictions.
  • Exposure of privacy preferences and security settings.
  • Improper enforcement of privacy and security policy.
  • DoS, such as directing a processor to send numerous responses to a client.
sections.plainLanguage: There is also a behind-the-scenes paper trail: bills, rules and settings. If someone messes with that, people get charged wrongly or their privacy wishes are ignored.
